..
Issued at 221 PM EST Tue Nov 3 2026

Now - Wednesday Night...

Mild and gusty this afternoon with temperatures approaching record 
highs in the upper 70s and low 80s as we speak. Gusts have mostly 
been in the 20-30 mph range, and will start to slacken by late 
afternoon. Otherwise, look for increasing mid and upper sky cover, 
but conditions will stay dry through sunset.

Records:

SDF - 82 (2003) 
LEX - 78 (2024) 
BWG - 82 (1974)

As we move through tonight, expect intense low level jetting to 
increase up around 50-60 knots beneath the right entrance region of 
strong mid to upper level jetting (70+ knots). Meanwhile, a surface 
cold front will approach the lower Ohio/Wabash River Valleys by dawn 
on Wednesday. This will provide the setup for widespread rainfall 
later tonight into Wednesday as forcing from the dynamics mentioned 
above combine with high PWATs (1.6 - 1.7"). It is worth noting that 
the low level jet fetch does appear to tap into an Atlantic and Gulf 
moisture feed in addition to the deep moisture already associated 
with this system. Precipitation has trended with an earlier start 
time tonight (likely some scattered showers before Midnight EST), 
likely due to that combined moisture fetch from the western 
Atlantic/eastern Gulf initially before the main plume arrives a bit 
later.

Although the widespread rainfall will be beneficial to ongoing 
drought conditions, especially southern KY where D1-D2 is currently 
observed. There are going to be a couple of concerns as we navigate 
the system later tonight through much of the daylight hours on 
Wednesday. Recent model runs have trended more aggressive with 
overall rainfall totals as a few hundred J/KG of MUCAPE allows for 
some convective elements in the presence of high PWATs. Previous 
discussion mentioned a seasonably deep warm cloud layer combined 
with some training potential could lead to localized high amounts. 
We're seeing this in the CAM data has the latest runs of the REFs 
suggest localized amounts over 4" on the 48 hour PMM data. This may 
very well be weighted a bit too heavy from the FV3 and WRF ARW, but 
also can't rule it out given that NBM probabilities of > 4" through 
tomorrow have risen to around 10%, and probabilities over 3" are 
about 20-30% across south central KY. Given all this for 
consideration, like the messaging of a widespread 1 to 2", with 
localized amounts of 3-4" possible. For the most part, we should be 
able to handle these amounts, however the higher end could cause a 
few localized issues, especially in urban areas. The good news is 
that the signal for the highest totals does seem to line out with 
the worst current drought conditions.

The overall shear profile later tonight into Wednesday is quite 
impressive given the strong low level jet, and somewhat backed 
surface winds. The good news is that any surface or near-surface 
based instability looks to be pretty much non-existent. This will 
mostly mitigate the threat for any of the higher momentum air aloft 
to make it down to the surface with stronger showers/storms. That 
being said, can't completely rule out a few stronger gusts over 40 
mph possible early Wednesday through the afternoon. REFS probs of 
500 J/KG of SB CAPE do show a few pixels of 5-10% over southern KY 
tomorrow afternoon ahead of the front, so something we'll have to 
watch. SPC did bring a 2% Tor threat up to our SW CWA border, and 
could see a sliver of this threat extending into south central KY 
into Wed, but not sure the threat is even that high. Will call it 
non-zero for a brief spin-up, but not likely at all given the low 
level thermodynamic profile evident on soundings.

Thursday - Tuesday...

General troughing will continue to hold over the region through the 
late week time frame, ending with a closed upper low slowly exiting 
the eastern Great Lakes into the weekend. Expect this to be mostly 
dry stretch with the bulk of the data keeping the deeper moisture 
far enough north that we stay dry. Do expect some increases in cloud 
cover, especially as the trough axis and weak frontal boundary 
passes Friday.

Temperatures are expected to trend downward Thursday through 
Saturday with successive reinforcing (but dry) cool fronts. Highs in 
the upper 60s to around 70 on Thursday will give way to highs only 
in the 55 to 60 degree range by Saturday. Thursday night lows look 
to be in the 40s with Friday night lows more into the 30s to around 
40. Some frost is likely for early Saturday morning. Same as we 
trended downward with temps through Saturday, they will then trend 
steadily warmer Sunday through Tuesday, ending up back in the mid 
60s by early to middle next week. 

This should also continue to be a dry stretch of weather as 
unremarkable NW flow aloft and high pressure at the surface control 
the area.
